subject: Earth & space

legend.name: Delta
legend.meaning: New land built of river sand and mud

legend.name: Ocean
legend.meaning: Still water where the river slows

note.text: Rock high in the mountains is weathered: broken into pieces by ice, water and plant roots.

steps.title: River
steps.instruction: Trace the river winding down from the mountains.

note.text: Fast-flowing water erodes: it picks up rock pieces and carries them away. Faster water can carry bigger pieces.

steps.title: Carrying sediment
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow showing sediment moving downstream.

note.text: Sand and mud travel with the water, sometimes for hundreds of kilometres.

steps.title: Ocean
steps.instruction: Trace the coastline and the ocean.

note.text: Where the river meets still water, it slows down and can't carry its load any more.

steps.title: Delta
steps.instruction: Trace the fan of land where the river meets the ocean.

note.text: The dropped sediment builds new land: a delta. Dropping sediment is called deposition.

steps.title: Channels
steps.instruction: Draw the three channels spreading across the delta.

note.text: The river splits into channels that spread sediment across the delta, making it grow out into the sea.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the mountains, the ocean and the delta.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why does the river drop its sediment at the coast?

options.text: The water slows down when it enters the still ocean
options.feedback: Yes. Slower water can't hold up as much sediment, so the sand and mud settle out and build the delta.

options.text: The water speeds up at the coast
options.feedback: It's the opposite: the river slows down, and slow water drops its sediment.
Salt doesn't dissolve sand. The river slows down and drops it.
The sediment settles because the water slows down when it reaches the ocean.

steps.title: Time scale
steps.question: Most of the land on the Fraser River delta in Canada formed in the last 10,000 years. What does this show?

options.text: Slow, steady deposition can build a lot of new land over thousands of years
options.feedback: Right. A little sediment each year adds up: whole towns now stand on land the river built.

options.text: Deltas form in a single day
options.feedback: Deltas grow bit by bit. The Fraser delta took about 10,000 years.
Rivers do both: they erode upstream and deposit downstream, building deltas.
This delta shows land changing a lot, slowly, over thousands of years.
